item.title: Why I Chose Baserow Over Airtable and Others
item.description:
For my automation project, I needed a data layer that felt local, predictable, and easy to connect to workflows. The shortlist was Airtable, Notion, Supabase, and Baserow.

Airtable was tempting because it appears in almost every automation tutorial. Notion looked friendly too. But both rely on hosted services, and that does not fit a local-first system where I want control over availability, limits, and data.

Why Baserow fit

Supabase is powerful, but it felt like more infrastructure than I needed for this particular workflow. Baserow landed in the middle: a spreadsheet-style interface, a clear API, Docker-friendly self-hosting, and a model that makes sense alongside n8n.

item.title: Setting Up My First Baserow Stack With YouTube and AI
item.description:
I wanted a local foundation for content automation: a place to store data, files, and workflow state without handing the whole system to a hosted platform. The stack became Baserow, MinIO, n8n, and local AI tools.

YouTube tutorials helped me see the broad shape of Baserow, but the useful learning started when I had to make the pieces talk to each other. Docker networks, environment variables, internal URLs, ports, Redis, PostgreSQL, storage, and API credentials all became less abstract once I had to troubleshoot them.

item.title: My First n8n & Ollama Experiment (and the Telegram Bot Mess)
item.description:
My first n8n experiment was meant to be simple: connect a local Ollama model, build a small workflow, then let a Telegram bot talk to it.

The first part worked. Docker Desktop ran both containers, n8n connected to Ollama, and I could send prompts through a workflow. It was slow without GPU acceleration, but it was real progress.

Where the plan met the network

Telegram needs a public, secure URL for its trigger. My temporary Windows and Docker setup did not have one. I had no router access for port forwarding, no stable external address, and no sensible reason to force a reverse proxy into a network I did not control.

item.title: Hosting My First Local AI: The Ollama Experiment
item.description:
With Docker already running on my temporary setup, I wanted to try something more ambitious: hosting an AI model locally. The long-term idea is a private assistant that can fit into my own workflow without depending entirely on a cloud service.

I compared Ollama, Hugging Face, and LM Studio. Ollama won because it felt approachable while still fitting the Docker-based environment I was learning.

From terminal to a usable workspace

Ollama came up quickly in a container. The next improvement was Open WebUI, which gave me a browser-based chat interface for managing models and conversations locally. It made the experiment feel less like a command-line test and more like something I could use.

item.title: Going Down the Self-Hosted Notes Rabbit Hole
item.description:
I wanted a note-taking system that could grow with me: cross-platform, capable of syncing, comfortable with Markdown, and flexible enough for mind maps and project notes.

That led me through Simplenote, Obsidian, Evernote, Joplin, Notion, and Zoho Notebook. I compared them through the things that mattered to me: cost, offline access, privacy, plugins, syncing, and whether the tool could eventually live in a self-hosted setup.

Choosing for the long term

The shortlist became Obsidian and Joplin. Obsidian has a strong ecosystem, but Joplin felt closer to the system I wanted to build: open source, Markdown-first, self-hostable, and able to sync through services such as Nextcloud.

item.title: Fixing Mounting Issues – A Deeper Dive Into the Solution
item.description:
When the portable-cloud idea failed, I stopped treating the SSD as the problem and started looking at the roles I had given everything. The drive was being asked to behave like portable storage, a Docker volume, and the home for a database-backed service at the same time.

Windows, WSL, and Linux all mounted it differently. That meant changing paths, inconsistent permissions, and containers that could not reliably find the data they needed. Nextcloud needed stability; the SSD was built to move.

item.title: The Portable Cloud Experiment – A Failed Attempt
item.description:
I wanted a cloud I could carry: an external SSD with Nextcloud, Syncthing, and Tailscale ready to run whenever I moved between machines. The idea was appealing—plug it in, start Docker, and keep the same environment everywhere.

Syncthing and Tailscale behaved well. Nextcloud did not. Its database, permissions, and storage expectations need a stable home. Windows, WSL, and Linux mounted the SSD differently; paths changed, permissions changed, and Docker volumes became unpredictable.

item.title: The Learning of Linux Commands and the Unexpected Pause
item.description:
Just as I was ready to spend more time with Linux, I had to lend my main computer to a friend. The hands-on homelab work paused, but I did not want the learning to pause with it.

So I made a smaller environment on my laptop: Docker Desktop with WSL2 and Ubuntu. It is not the final home lab, but it gives me somewhere safe to test ideas while the main machine is away.

item.title: From Proxmox Dreams to Ubuntu Reality
item.description:
With hardware sorted, I reached the next big choice: the operating system. Proxmox kept appearing in homelab guides, and I understood why. It is capable, popular, and built for the virtualised setup I hoped to grow into.

The installation itself went smoothly. The problem appeared afterwards. My internet connection relies on a captive portal, and the combination of missing Wi-Fi drivers, no easy way to authenticate, and limited access to the packages I needed turned a simple install into a loop.

item.title: When Research Meets Reality: My Unexpected Home Lab Setup?
item.description:
I began looking for homelab hardware convinced I wanted a Raspberry Pi. I had used one at school, liked the size, and assumed it was the natural place to start.

Then I did the maths. A newer Pi was already stretching my budget, and the power supply, storage, enclosure, cooling, and other extras made the total less appealing. I compared SBCs and mini PCs and learned that the “cheap” option depends on the whole setup—not just the headline price.

item.title: My First Step in Setting Up a Home Lab
item.description:
My first home-lab step was not buying hardware or running a container. It was admitting that I had a lot to learn.

I started with a simple idea: create one place for the tools, files, and experiments scattered across my devices. Research quickly showed me that a home lab can be whatever you need it to be—a place to learn Linux, host useful services, test automation, or simply understand your own technology better.

item.title: 🚧 The False Start to My Homelab Journey (Before I Knew What It Was)
item.description:
I did not set out to build a homelab. I just wanted my files to follow me between devices without becoming another thing to manage.

That small problem sent me through Syncthing, Joplin, WSL2, Docker, Nextcloud, and Tailscale. Each tool solved part of the problem, but I was trying to assemble a complete system before I understood the pieces.

The first attempt

I tried to turn Docker and WSL2 into a private cloud, with Nextcloud at the centre. It sounded sensible: build something portable now, then move it to future hardware later. In practice, containers failed to start, storage paths became confusing, and VPN conflicts made even basic setup work harder than it should have been.
